name: Alpes Maritimes
subtitle: Provence & the Riviera

days.title: Bremen → Sospel
days.detail: The big one. ~1 450 km via Basel, Bern and the Rhône valley — two drivers, 05:00 start, camp by dusk. If that sounds brutal, break it near Beaune and arrive midday on the 8th; you lose half a riding day but nobody arrives wrecked.

days.title: Col de Turini
days.detail: The Monte Carlo Rally stage — 34 hairpins up from Sospel. Then Peïra-Cava, Col Saint-Roch, the hill village of Lucéram, home over Col de Braus. Short distance, enormous amount of cornering.

days.title: Gorges du Loup & the Corniches
days.detail: West to Col de Vence and the cliff village of Gourdon, down the Gorges du Loup, then back east along the three Corniches above Monaco. Ride the Corniches late — the light is better and the traffic has gone.

days.title: Sospel → Castellane
days.detail: Strike camp, ~150 km inland via Grasse. Pitch by early afternoon, then a shakeout run north on the Route Napoléon.

days.title: Gorges du Verdon circuit
days.detail: The Route des Crêtes (D23) is one-way and rides clockwise — do it first, early. Then the Corniche Sublime along the south rim, around Lac de Sainte-Croix and back via Moustiers. Slow going: you will stop constantly.

days.title: Gorges du Cians & Daluis
days.detail: North-east via Entrevaux into the red-rock gorges — Daluis up, Cians down, or the reverse. Deep red schist, tunnels cut straight through the rock. The best-kept secret of the region.

days.title: Castellane → Cassis
days.detail: ~190 km south-west to the coast. Once the tent is up, ride the Route des Crêtes over Cap Canaille — the highest sea cliffs in France, and about 20 minutes from camp.

days.title: Sainte-Baume & the Var coast
days.detail: Inland over the Sainte-Baume massif, down the Gorges d'Ollioules, then the coast road through Bandol, Sanary and Six-Fours. Note the Calanques themselves are closed to vehicles — they are a walk, not a ride.

days.title: Cassis → Luberon
days.detail: ~130 km north to Bonnieux or Apt. Afternoon loop through the perched villages: Lourmarin, Ménerbes, Gordes, Roussillon.

days.title: Mont Ventoux & Gorges de la Nesque
days.detail: Up the classic Bédoin side, down to Malaucène, across the Sault plateau and back through the Gorges de la Nesque. Check the summit road before you set off — it closes for wind more often than people expect.

days.title: Luberon → Bremen
days.detail: ~1 250 km home, 200 km shorter than the way down. That is the whole reason for running the route east to west.

campsites.name: Camping Domaine Sainte Madeleine
campsites.note: On the Route du Moulinet — already pointing at Turini. No barbecues. Mountain site, so it closes earlier than the coast: confirm before you rely on it.

campsites.name: Camping Chasteuil Verdon Provence
campsites.note: On the D952, about 15 minutes from Point Sublime. The other mountain site — same closing-date question as Sospel.

campsites.name: Camping Ceyreste
campsites.note: Between Cassis and La Ciotat, right by the Route des Crêtes.

campsites.name: Camping Le Luberon / Pausado
campsites.note: Near Apt, so closer to Ventoux than a Bonnieux pitch would be. Confirmed open late season.

rejectedCampsites: Le Mas Fleuri — late-September cleanliness reports
La Ferme de Castellane — rated higher, but badly placed for the Verdon
Le Vallon du Luberon — small pitches, hot water complaints
campsiteCaveat: Coastal campsites in Brittany and Normandy close between 15 and 30 September — the Bayeux end of Plan A sits inside that window. Provence runs later, but the mountain sites at Sospel and Castellane close earlier than the coast. No closing date here has been confirmed. These need phone calls, not more reading.

items.title: Four reflective stickers per helmet
items.why: Front, back and both sides, at least 18 cm² each. Without them a helmet counts as unapproved in France — €135. Applies to foreign riders too.

items.title: CE-approved gloves, rider and pillion
items.why: Mandatory since 2016. Ordinary gloves do not count — look for the CE / EN 13594 mark.

items.title: Hi-vis vest per rider, reachable from the saddle
items.why: The law says within reach while seated, so tank bag or under the seat — not buried in a pannier. Fine rises sharply if you are stopped at the roadside without it.

items.title: Dipped headlight on at all times
items.why: Required day and night for motorcycles.

items.title: Crit’Air sticker — you will need one
items.why: Nice, Marseille, Aix and Toulon all run low-emission zones and you ride through that arc repeatedly. Order online weeks ahead; it costs a few euros and arrives by post.

items.title: Insurance certificate for each bike
items.why: A green card is no longer needed between EU countries, but carry your Versicherungsbestätigung anyway — it settles roadside questions fast.

items.title: Insurance for the bikes while inside the transporter
items.why: The gap people miss. Many motor policies do not cover a bike being carried as cargo. Confirm with your insurer in writing before you load.

items.title: Zulassungsbescheinigung Teil I for every vehicle
items.why: Bikes and the transporter.

items.title: Driving licences and ID or passports
EHIC / European health card
items.why: On the back of your German Krankenkasse card.

items.title: Breakdown cover valid in France, including bike recovery
items.why: Check the policy covers a motorcycle and, separately, the transporter.

items.title: Written permission if you ride a bike registered to someone else
Ratchet straps and soft loops
items.why: Four points per bike. Soft loops save your bars and fork tubes.

items.title: Front wheel chock or a proper front strap setup
Check total weight and axle load with bikes aboard
Somewhere secure to leave the empty van at each campsite
items.why: Ask when booking — some sites charge for a second vehicle or cap length.

items.title: Tyres with real tread left
items.why: Hot tarmac and hairpins chew edges. You are cornering hard for ten days — start with more tread than you think you need.

items.title: Puncture repair kit and a mini compressor
Basic tools and a spare clutch or brake lever
Chain lube
items.why: Coastal salt air and rain will strip it inside a week.

items.title: Rain gear you actually trust
items.why: Not for drizzle — for a Mediterranean downpour that arrives in ten minutes.

items.title: Both warm and vented layers
items.why: 28 °C in the Rhône valley, 10 °C at the top of Ventoux or Turini, on the same day. You need the full range.

items.title: Clear visor and a tinted one
items.why: Harsh southern glare by day, but the gorges go dark early.

items.title: Tent that handles wind, plus rock pegs
items.why: Provençal ground is stony and hard — soft alloy pegs bend. The mistral will find any weakness in a pitch.

items.title: Campsite closing dates confirmed
items.why: Provence runs later than the Atlantic — many sites stay open to mid-October — but mountain sites at Sospel and Castellane close earlier. Confirm those two.

items.title: Camping gas — buy in France
items.why: Cartridges cannot legally travel in the van. Pick up locally. Note fire restrictions may ban open flames in the Var in dry spells.

items.title: Cash and a second bank card
items.why: Rural French pumps are card-only after hours and sometimes reject foreign cards. Do not let the tank get low on a Sunday evening.

items.title: Offline maps downloaded
items.why: No signal at the bottom of the Verdon, the Cians or the Daluis.

items.title: Sunscreen and a hydration pack
items.why: Early September in Provence still runs to 30 °C. Dehydration creeps up on you inside riding gear.

items.title: Autoroute toll payment sorted
items.why: The van run down is heavily tolled — roughly €120 each way in France. Carry a card that works at unmanned barriers, plus cash.

items.title: Météo-France vigilance app installed
items.why: Orange and red alerts for storms are issued by département and are the fastest way to know a riding day is off.

items.title: Emergency number 112, and a contact left at home
